title: The GPU in omxcode
subtitle: The pixel function is plain Mojo in app.mojo; omxcode makes it a kernel; the platform's own widgets show the picture

floors.label: Mojo
floors.note: one file, one language, one compiler

nodes.label: Pixel function
nodes.desc: An ordinary Mojo function in the app's own file: the colour of one pixel. No kernel syntax, no shader language.

nodes.label: view()
nodes.desc: The picture is one more thing on the screen: a Canvas node next to the sliders and buttons.

nodes.label: gpu.draw[f]
nodes.desc: gpu.draw[f]: wraps the function in a kernel (one GPU thread per pixel) and launches it through MAX's DeviceContext, at the canvas's real size.

nodes.label: render_on_cpu[f]
nodes.desc: Runs the same function on the CPU, one pixel at a time. examples/gpu uses it to check the GPU's picture pixel for pixel. The framework's drawing types (PointCloud, tables) fall back to it when there is no GPU.

nodes.label: diff()
nodes.desc: The same diff as every other screen change.

nodes.label: MAX
nodes.desc: Compiles the Mojo kernel for the GPU and launches it. omxcode's GPU drawing builds for Linux; elsewhere the framework's drawing types use the CPU.

nodes.label: Main memory (fallback)
nodes.desc: Where the host can't take a GPU picture yet (the Mac, the web, a display without GL), the pixels are copied to main memory and the toolkit uploads them again. The best GPU apps never do this.

nodes.label: GL texture
nodes.desc: The default for GPU apps on GTK with NVIDIA: the picture stays on the GPU and is copied GPU to GPU into an OpenGL texture GTK shows (CUDA–GL interop, mojoui/present.mojo).

nodes.label: Native image view
nodes.desc: Each platform's own image widget shows the picture, beside its own buttons.

nodes.label: Toolkit renderer
nodes.desc: The toolkit composites the window on the GPU itself, as it does for every app.

steps.note: mandelbrot(x, y, …) is a plain Mojo function in app.mojo: the colour of one pixel.
omxcode wraps it in a kernel. MAX compiles it for the GPU: no nvcc, no .cu file.
Mac and web, for now: the pixels are copied to main memory. The best GPU apps keep them in GPU memory.
They fill a Canvas in view(), like any other part of the screen.
The usual diff: only the picture changed.
The platform's own image view shows it, next to its own buttons.
The toolkit composites the window on the GPU, as it does for every app.
On screen. One language from the slider to the kernel.

flows.name: Linux + NVIDIA: stays on the GPU

steps.note: An app that declares GPU_CANVAS draws the same way.
The picture is copied GPU to GPU into an OpenGL texture: CUDA–GL interop, no CPU copy.
GTK's own picture widget shows that texture. Linux, NVIDIA and GTK's GL renderer only; examples/particles uses it today.

flows.name: The same function on the CPU

steps.note: render_on_cpu[mandelbrot] runs the very same function on the CPU.
examples/gpu compares both pictures pixel for pixel. No second version to keep in step.
